# Tools

## R
::: {.incremental}
- [posterior](https://mc-stan.org/posterior/): Conversion, manipulation, and summarization of draws from posterior and prior distributions.
- [bayesplot](https://mc-stan.org/bayesplot/): Visual checks and summaries.
- [loo](https://mc-stan.org/loo/): Model comparison using leave-one-out cross-validation and related methods.
- [priorsense](https://n-kall.github.io/priorsense/): Prior diagnostics and sensitivity analysis.

:::

## Python
::: {.incremental}
- [arviz-base](https://python.arviz.org/projects/base/en/latest/): Data related functionality, including converters from different PPLs.
- [arviz-stats](https://python.arviz.org/projects/stats/en/latest/): Statistical functions and diagnostics.
- [arviz-plots](https://python.arviz.org/projects/plots/en/latest/): Visual checks and summaries built on top of arviz-stats and arviz-base.
- [arviz](https://python.arviz.org/en/latest/): a meta-package that imports all the above and provides a single namespace for users.

:::

# Posterior objects

## Data structures
::: {.incremental}

- `posterior` provides objects for draws that mimic built-in types: `matrix`, `array`, `data.frame`, `list`
- `arviz` uses xarray's `DataTree` object for posterior draws (and other related data, like posterior predictive draws and observed data).

:::

# Convergence and uncertainty

## R-hat
::: {.incremental}
- Convergence diagnostic
- Measure of ratio between within-chain and between-chain variance
- R-hat > 1.01 indicates lack of convergence
:::
## R-hat
```{r}
sample <- readRDS("../models/prerun/sample.rds")
summarise_draws(sample, rhat) |>
tt(digits = 3)
```

## Nested R-hat
::: {.incremental}
- Convergence diagnostic when using many short chains
- Chains are grouped into superchains (sharing initialization)
- Classic R-hat may wrongly indicate lack of convergence, but nested R-hat does not
:::
## Nested R-hat
```{r}
#| echo: false
many_short_chains <- readRDS("../models/prerun/many_short_chains.rds")

summarise_draws(
    many_short_chains,
    rhat,
    nested_rhat = ~ rhat_nested(.x, superchain_ids = attr(many_short_chains, "superchain_ids"))
) |>
tt() |>
format_tt(digits = 3, num_fmt = "decimal")
```


## Effective Sample Size

::: {.incremental}

- Measures how much *independent* information the draws contain
- Accounts for autocorrelation between samples
- `ess_bulk`: precision for mean/median (central distribution)
- `ess_tail`: precision for interval estimates (5%/95% quantiles)
- Rule of thumb: at least 400 total (100 per chain x 4 chains) for both
:::
## Effective Sample Size
```{r}
summarise_draws(sample, ess_bulk, ess_tail) |>
  tt() |>
  format_tt(j = c("ess_bulk", "ess_tail"), fn = function(x) sprintf("%.0f", x)) |>
  style_tt(j = c("ess_bulk", "ess_tail"), align = "r")
```


## Monte Carlo Standard Error

::: {.incremental}

- Standard error of a posterior estimate (e.g. the mean), accounting for autocorrelation
- Related to ESS: $\text{MCSE} = \frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{\text{ESS}}}$
- Tells us [how many digits](https://avehtari.github.io/Bayesian-Workflow/digits/digits.html) of a reported estimate we can trust
:::
## Monte Carlo Standard Error
```{r}
summarise_draws(sample, mcse_mean) |>
  tt() |>
  format_tt(j = c("mcse_mean"), fn = function(x) sprintf("%.4f", x)) |>
  style_tt(j = c("mcse_mean"), align = "r")
```


## Pareto-$\hat{k}$

::: {.incremental}

- Quantifies whether the tails are too heavy to trust the mean/MCSE
- Fits a generalized Pareto distribution to the tail, $\hat k$ estimates tail heaviness
- Converts to a minimum sample size to trust MCSE: $10^{1 / (1 - \max(0, \hat{k}))}$
- If $\hat{k} \geq 1$: the mean doesn't exist (no amount of sampling helps)

:::

## Pareto-$\hat{k}$
```{r}
drt <- readRDS("../models/prerun/drt.rds")
summarise_draws(drt, mcse_mean, ess_mean, min_ss = pareto_min_ss) |> 
  tt() |>
  format_tt(j = c("mcse_mean", "ess_mean"), fn = function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)) |>
  format_tt(j = c("min_ss"), fn = function(x) sprintf("%.0f", x)) |>
  style_tt(j = c("mcse_mean", "ess_mean", "min_ss"), align = "r")

```

# Model evaluation and critique

# Predictive checks
::: {.incremental}
- Models are simplifications — judge them by their predictions
- Four ways to check predictions: prior knowledge, observed data, unobserved data, other models
- Two types of predictions: **prior predictive** (before seeing data) and **posterior predictive** (after seeing data)
:::
## Prior predictive checks
::: {.incremental}
- Generate synthetic data from the prior, *before* looking at observed data
- Algorithm: sample $\theta \sim p(\theta)$ → simulate $y \sim p(y \mid \theta)$ → compare to domain knowledge
- Judged against domain knowledge, **not** observed data
:::

## 
```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Prior predictive check for heights: bulk of mass falls outside plausible range."
data <- readRDS("../models/prerun/00.rds")
ppd_dens_overlay(data$prior_predictive) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(50, 182), linetype = "dashed")
```

## Weakly informative priors
::: {.incremental}
- Vague priors can produce implausible predictions (e.g. negative heights)
- Weakly informative priors: little/no mass in impossible regions, but not overly restrictive
- Benefits: guards against implausible results, can improve sampling efficiency, easier to elicit than fully informative priors
:::

## 
```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Prior predictive check with a tighter, weakly informative prior."
data <- readRDS("../models/prerun/01.rds")
ppd_dens_overlay(data$prior_predictive) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(50, 182), linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(45, NA))
```


## Posterior predictive checks
::: {.incremental}
- Generate synthetic data from the posterior, *after* fitting the model
- Algorithm: sample $\theta \sim p(\theta \mid y)$ → simulate $\tilde y \sim p(\tilde y \mid \theta)$ → compare to **observed** data
- A more stringent test than prior predictive checks
:::
## 
```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Posterior predictive check: observed data (black) vs. predictive draws (blue)."
data <- readRDS("../models/prerun/02.rds")
ppc_dens_overlay(data$observed_data, data$posterior_predictive[1:200, ])
```


## Posterior predictive checks: summary statistics
::: {.incremental}
- Compare observed vs. predicted **test statistics** (median, MAD, IQR, ...) instead of full densities
- Choose statistics orthogonal to model parameters (e.g. avoid the mean for a location-parameter model - it's trivially recovered)
:::
## 
```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Posterior predictive check using median, MAD, and IQR as test statistics."
y    <- data$observed_data
yrep <- data$posterior_predictive

p1 <- ppc_stat(y, yrep, stat = "median")
p2 <- ppc_stat(y, yrep, stat = "mad")
p3 <- ppc_stat(y, yrep, stat = "IQR")

bayesplot_grid(p1, p2, p3, grid_args = list(nrow = 1))
```

## Posterior predictive p-values
::: {.incremental}
- $p(T_{\text{sim}} \leq T_{\text{obs}} \mid \tilde y)$ - proportion of simulated statistics below the observed one
- 0.5 = predictions split evenly around the observation
- Not uniform under the null - tend to concentrate near 0.5
- Used as a **diagnostic**, not a significance test
:::
## PIT-ECDFs
::: {.incremental}
- Marginal p-value: $p(\tilde y_i \leq y_i \mid y)$, computed per observation
- By the Probability Integral Transform, this should be **standard Uniform** if model and data agree
- Compare the empirical CDF of these values to the diagonal line
:::
## 
```{r}
#| fig-cap: "PIT-ECDF (Δ-ECDF) for the heights model."
ppc_pit_ecdf(data$observed_data, data$posterior_predictive,
             method = "correlated", plot_diff = TRUE)
```

## PIT-ECDF: why the Δ version?
::: {.incremental}
- Plain ECDF vs. diagonal wastes space — all the signal sits near the line
- **Δ-ECDF**: plot the *difference* from the uniform CDF instead
- Ideal Δ-ECDF: flat line at zero; deviations show as peaks/valleys
- Complement with a uniformity test to judge if deviations exceed what's expected by chance
:::
## PIT-ECDF quartet
::: {.incremental}
- Four miscalibration patterns, compared via KDE (left) vs. PIT-ECDF (right)
  - Predictions shifted right → overprediction
  - Predictions shifted left → underprediction
  - Predictions too spread out → overdispersed
  - Predictions too narrow → overconfident
- PIT-ECDF is more sensitive to subtle miscalibration than KDEs/histograms
:::
## 
```{r}
#| fig-cap: "KDE and PIT-ECDF comparison across four miscalibration scenarios."
data_i <- readRDS("../models/prerun/pit_ecdf_quartet.rds")
vars <- c("y0", "y1", "y2", "y3")

plots <- do.call(c, lapply(vars, function(v) {
  y <- data_i$observed_data[[v]]
  yrep <- as_draws_matrix(data_i$posterior_predictive[[v]])

  list(
    ppc_dens_overlay(y, yrep[1:50, ]),
    ppc_pit_ecdf(y, yrep, method = "correlated", plot_diff = TRUE)
  )
}))

patchwork::wrap_plots(plots, ncol = 2, axes = "collect", guides = "collect")
```

## Avoiding double-dipping
::: {.incremental}
- So far: data used twice (fit *and* check) - generally fine, but a more stringent test exists
- Leave-one-out: $p(\tilde y_i \leq y_i \mid y_{-i})$ instead of $p(\tilde y_i \leq y_i \mid y)$
- Exact LOO-CV is expensive ($n$ refits) → approximate with **Pareto-smoothed importance sampling (PSIS)**
:::

# 
```{r}
#| fig-cap: "LOO-PIT-ECDF for the heights model."
psis_result <- psis(-data$log_likelihood)
lw <- psis_result$log_weights
ppc_loo_pit_ecdf(data$observed_data, data$posterior_predictive, lw,
                  method = "correlated", plot_diff = TRUE)
```

## Predictive checks for discrete data
::: {.incremental}
- KDEs don't work well for discrete data (unless enough distinct values to treat as continuous)
- Histograms (one bin per value) and ECDFs still apply
- Some tools are purpose-built per data type: **count**, **binary**, **categorical**, **ordinal**, **censored**
:::
## Count data: rootograms
::: {.incremental}
- Rootograms compare observed vs. predicted counts, on a **square-root** y-axis (easier to compare low frequencies)
- Points = predictions with uncertainty intervals; markers = observed counts
:::

## 
```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Rootogram for the Poisson model of crab satellites."
crabs_poisson <- readRDS("../models/prerun/crabs_poisson.rds")
ppc_rootogram(crabs_poisson$observed_data, crabs_poisson$posterior_predictive, style = "discrete") +
coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 20))
```


## 
```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Rootogram for the Hurdle Negative Binomial model of crab satellites."
crabs_hurdle_nb <- readRDS("../models/prerun/crabs_hurdle_nb.rds")
ppc_rootogram(crabs_hurdle_nb$observed_data, crabs_hurdle_nb$posterior_predictive, style = "discrete") +
coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 20))
```

## Binary data: calibration plots
::: {.incremental}
- Bar plots don't work - even trivial models can match the observed proportion
- Bin predicted probabilities → compare to observed frequency per bin (traditional calibration plot)
- Binning is arbitrary and unstable → prefer a binning-free method (Dimitriadis et al.)
- Ideal plot: diagonal line. Above diagonal = underestimating; below = overestimating
:::

##
```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Calibration plot for the ANES model of voting behavior."
anes <- readRDS("../models/prerun/anes.rds")
ppc_calibration(anes$observed_data,
                anes$posterior,
                interval = "consistency"
              )
```


## Categorical data
::: {.incremental}
- One-vs-others strategy: pick one category, compare it to "everything else" — repeat per category
- Manageable for few categories; use a confusion matrix or scalar miscalibration summary to triage which categories to inspect visually when there are many
:::
<!-- We need new unreleased version of bayesplot -->


## Ordinal data
::: {.incremental}
- Categories have a natural order, but unknown distances between them
- Must account for order: compute **cumulative** conditional event probabilities
- Yields one fewer plot than the number of categories
:::
<!-- We need new unreleased version of bayesplot -->


## Censored data
::: {.incremental}
- Survival/time-to-event models: some events not yet observed at data-collection time
- Naively discarding censored cases biases the estimate
- Replace raw observations with **Kaplan–Meier** estimates for posterior predictive checks
:::
## 
```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Posterior predictive check for cat adoption times using Kaplan–Meier curves."
cens <- readRDS("../models/prerun/censored_cats.rds")
ppc_km_overlay(cens$observed_data, cens$posterior_predictive[1:50, ],
               status_y = cens$constant_data)
```

# Sensitivity checks
## Power-scaling sensitivity
::: {.incremental}
- What would happen if the prior was weaker or stronger?

- $p(\theta \mid y) \propto p(\theta)^{\alpha} p(y \mid \theta)$

- What about the likelihood?

- $p(\theta \mid y) \propto p(\theta) p(y \mid \theta)^{\alpha}$
:::

## Visual checks
```{r}
#| echo: false
theme_set(bayesplot::theme_default(base_family = "sans", base_size = 14))
norm_ps <- example_powerscale_model()$draws

powerscale_plot_dens(norm_ps, component = "prior", variable = "mu", help_text = FALSE)

```

## Numerical checks
Values > 0.05 indicate sensitivity
```{r}
powerscale_sensitivity(norm_ps, prior_selection = "mu") |>
tt(digits = 1)

```
